title: Spinoza
orientation: Russell presents Baruch Spinoza (1634-77) as ethically the greatest of the philosophers even though his metaphysics cannot be accepted. This chapter traces how Spinoza reworked Descartes's dualism into a single infinite substance ('God or Nature') and built on that austere metaphysics an ethic of intellectual acceptance, aimed at freeing human beings from fear, hatred, and the tyranny of hope and dread.
historical_background: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam to a Portuguese/Spanish Jewish family that had fled the Inquisition. Educated in Jewish learning, he was excommunicated by the Amsterdam Jewish community for his heterodox views, survived an assassination attempt, and refused a bribe to conceal his doubts. He lived simply, polishing lenses for a living, in a Dutch Republic whose relative religious toleration let him work and publish (mostly posthumously) despite being reviled by Jews and Christians alike as an atheist.
philosophical_problems: How many fundamental substances exist, and how are mind and matter related to them?
Is there free will, or does absolute logical necessity govern everything, including human choice?
How can evil and sin be reconciled with a universe wholly determined by a perfect God?
What is the best way for a person to achieve freedom, and to bear misfortune, given that so much of life lies outside our control?

philosophers_discussed.name: Baruch Spinoza
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject; his life, his political writings, and above all the metaphysics, psychology of emotions, and ethics of the Ethics are examined in detail.

philosophers_discussed.name: Rene Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as the source of Spinoza's metaphysical starting point; Spinoza is shown reducing Descartes's three substances (God, mind, matter) to a single substance.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Russell notes that Spinoza's political theory in the Tractatus Politicus is derived mainly from Hobbes, though Spinoza departs from him on democracy and on subjects retaining some rights.

philosophers_discussed.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned as having owed much to Spinoza while concealing the debt and denying the extent of their personal acquaintance.

core_concepts.name: Substance monism ("God or Nature")
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Instead of Descartes's three separate substances (God, mind, matter), Spinoza holds there is only one substance in the whole universe, which he calls indifferently 'God' or 'Nature.' Everything else - every mind, every physical object - is not an independent thing but merely an aspect or 'mode' of this single infinite being.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that reality consists of a single, infinite, self-caused substance possessing infinitely many attributes (of which thought and extension are the only two known to us), and that all finite things are merely modes or adjectival aspects of that one substance.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It dissolves the mind-body dualism Descartes had left unresolved, but at the cost of denying that individual minds and bodies are truly separate, self-subsistent things.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell traces its lineage to Parmenides' doctrine that only one unchanging Being truly exists, and notes Spinoza inherited from Descartes the concepts of substance and attribute.
examples: An individual human soul is, for Spinoza, not a separate thing but an aspect of the one divine Being.
A piece of matter is likewise only an adjectival aspect of God/Nature, not an independent substance.
objections: Modern logic and scientific method reject the underlying theory that every proposition has a single subject and predicate, from which Spinoza's monism is derived, according to Russell.
It is incompatible with treating relations and plurality as ultimately real.
competing_positions: Descartes's dualism of three substances (God, mind, matter)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell calls Spinoza's system 'the best example' of logical monism, a type of philosophy that also runs through Parmenides, Plato's use of the theory of ideas, and later Hegel.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The doctrine that all things are aspects of God led directly to charges of atheism from Christians, even though Spinoza's entire philosophy is 'dominated by the idea of God.'

core_concepts.name: Determinism and the denial of free will
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Nothing that happens could have happened otherwise; everything, mental and physical, follows from God's nature with the same necessity that 2 and 2 make 4.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that all events, including human volitions, are governed by absolute logical necessity, so that chance and free will in the ordinary sense do not exist.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It creates the central puzzle of the chapter: how sin and evil can be meaningfully spoken of if everything is decreed by God and is, in that sense, 'good.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: A consequence Spinoza draws directly from his substance monism: since there is only one wholly positive Being, its acts cannot fail to occur as they do.
examples: Spinoza's answer to critics who asked whether it was 'good' that Nero killed his mother or that Adam ate the apple: what was positive in these acts was good, only the negative aspect (visible only from a finite viewpoint) appeared as evil.
objections: Contemporary critics pointed out this cannot be reconciled with the orthodox doctrine of sin and damnation.
Russell himself argues each act of cruelty is 'eternally a part of the universe' and does not become good by being absorbed into a supposed harmonious whole.
competing_positions: Christian doctrines of free will, sin, and damnation
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The rejection of free will was one of the chief reasons Spinoza was accused of impiety and atheism by his contemporaries.

core_concepts.name: All determination is negation
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anything finite is defined by its limits - by what it is not - so nothing finite can be wholly real or positive; only an infinite, unbounded being can be completely positive.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Spinoza's principle that finite things are individuated by their boundaries (physical or logical), which are a form of negation, so that only the single absolutely infinite substance is wholly positive.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the pivot of Spinoza's argument for pantheism: since only one being can be wholly positive, and everything positive must belong to it, that being must be absolutely infinite and singular.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Spinoza's own formulation, built on the logic of subject and predicate that Russell says underlies his whole metaphysic.

core_concepts.name: Bondage versus freedom / passions versus adequate ideas
core_concepts.plain_explanation: We are 'in bondage' when what happens to us is caused by things outside us and we do not understand why; we become 'free' as we understand our own emotions clearly, because a clearly and distinctly understood emotion stops being a passive 'passion.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Freedom, for Spinoza, consists in being self-determined through adequate understanding rather than driven by external causes grasped only through confused, inadequate ideas; an emotion ceases to be a 'passion' once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the psychological engine of Spinoza's ethics: intellectual understanding, not willpower or unselfishness, is presented as the remedy for destructive emotion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in the fourth and fifth books of the Ethics, 'Of Human Bondage' and 'Of the Power of the Understanding.'
examples: Hatred, once clearly understood in relation to its causes, loses its grip on the mind.
Hope and fear are condemned as irrational because they treat the future, which is really as fixed as the past, as uncertain.
competing_positions: The Stoics' rejection of all emotion, which Russell notes Spinoza does not share - Spinoza objects only to 'passions,' not to all feeling.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Compared by Russell to Socrates and Plato's view that wrong action stems from intellectual error.

core_concepts.name: The intellectual love of God (amor intellectualis Dei)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: As we come to understand more and more of reality as part of God, this growing understanding is itself accompanied by a special joy; this fusion of true thought and joy is what Spinoza calls the intellectual love of God, and he regards it as the highest human good.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A union of true understanding and joy that arises whenever the mind refers its ideas to God (i.e., understands them as part of the single, necessary whole); it is described as part of the infinite love with which God loves Himself.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Spinoza's substitute for personal immortality and conventional religious devotion, and the culminating good of the entire Ethics ('the mind's highest good is the knowledge of God').
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Book V of the Ethics, following a geometrical proof-style demonstration that Russell quotes in full.
examples: Russell quotes Spinoza's geometrical 'proof' that 'love towards God must hold the chief place in the mind.'
objections: Russell notes a tension: Spinoza says God feels no pleasure or pain, yet also speaks of joy in the intellectual love of God; Russell suggests the 'joy' here may be something superior to ordinary pleasure.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Goethe admired the related proposition that one who loves God cannot want God to love him in return, though Russell says Goethe misunderstood it as self-abnegation rather than logical necessity.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Substitutes for the Christian promise of personal immortality: what is eternal in the mind is this intellectual love, not a personal afterlife.

core_concepts.name: Sub specie aeternitatis (under the aspect of eternity)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The wise person tries to see events not as located at a particular, emotionally charged moment in time but as part of the timeless, eternal order that God sees - so a disaster today should not disturb us more than an equally bad disaster in the distant past.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Spinoza's principle that reason, so far as human limitation allows, views things as God does: timelessly, so that whether an idea concerns something present, past, or future makes no difference to the mind operating under the dictate of reason.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds Spinoza's rejection of hope and fear as irrational, since both depend on treating the future as uncertain rather than as fixed.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A direct consequence of Spinoza's determinism and his view that time itself is, in an important sense, unreal from God's perspective.
examples: Russell's counter-example: we are naturally more concerned about a disaster in our own time than one from the age of Genghis Khan, which Spinoza would call irrational.
objections: Russell argues this fails to distinguish future misfortunes we might still avert from past ones we cannot, though he notes Spinoza's determinism has a ready (if unconvincing) answer to this.

arguments.title: The argument from 'all determination is negation' to pantheistic monism
premises: Finite things are defined by their boundaries, which are a form of negation.
There can be only one being who is wholly positive.
A wholly positive being must be absolutely infinite.
arguments.conclusion: There is only one substance, absolutely infinite, which is God or Nature; nothing finite is self-subsistent.
arguments.explanation: Because every finite thing is marked off from others by what it lacks, no finite thing can be completely real in itself; only a being with no boundaries at all can be wholly positive, and there can only be one such being, since two infinite positive beings would limit each other.
objections: Russell says the whole metaphysic depends on an outdated logical assumption (that every proposition has a single subject and predicate) which modern logic rejects.
implications: Individual minds and bodies are not independent substances but modes of the one substance.
There can be no personal immortality, only an impersonal absorption into God.

arguments.title: Solution to the problem of evil via negation
premises: Everything that happens is a manifestation of God's nature and is therefore, in itself, necessary.
What is 'evil' in an act is only its negative aspect, which exists only from the limited viewpoint of finite creatures.
God, being wholly positive, has no knowledge of evil.
arguments.conclusion: Nothing bad can be said to happen to the universe as a whole, though from a finite, partial viewpoint certain acts appear evil.
arguments.explanation: Spinoza responds to critics who asked whether Nero's matricide or Adam's sin were 'good' by saying only the positive content of any act is real and good; the appearance of wrongness comes only from viewing a part in isolation from the whole.
objections: Russell rejects this personally: 'particular events are what they are, and do not become different by absorption into a whole,' and 'each act of cruelty is eternally a part of the universe.'
implications: Undermines the orthodox Christian doctrine of sin and damnation, which requires genuine moral responsibility and real evil.

arguments.title: Geometrical demonstration that 'love towards God must hold the chief place in the mind'
premises: The mind can refer all bodily modifications (images of things) to the idea of God (Ethics V, 14).
One who clearly and distinctly understands himself and his emotions loves God, more so as his understanding increases (Ethics V, 15).
A mental image occupies the mind more, and more frequently, the more objects it is referred to (Ethics V, 11).
arguments.conclusion: Love of God must hold the chief place in the mind.
arguments.explanation: Russell quotes the proof in full and paraphrases it: every increase in understanding consists in referring events to the idea of God (since everything is truly part of God); this understanding is itself love of God; and since all objects are eventually referred to God, the idea of God comes to occupy the mind fully.
implications: Shows that, for Spinoza, this claim is not a moral exhortation but a logically necessary consequence of his metaphysics, illustrating his geometrical method.

key_distinctions: Descartes's three substances (God, mind, matter) vs. Spinoza's single substance
Finite, negative/partial view vs. the infinite, wholly positive view of God
Personal immortality (rejected) vs. the impersonal eternal part of the mind
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces Spinoza's metaphysical style to Parmenides (logical monism) and describes his relation to Descartes as analogous to Plotinus's relation to Plato - a devout, morally serious successor systematizing a more freewheeling predecessor's ideas. His political theory borrows heavily from Hobbes.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Leibniz visited Spinoza in 1676, obtained part of the Ethics in manuscript, and was influenced by him, though he later downplayed the connection out of caution. Russell also groups Spinoza with Parmenides, Plato, and Hegel as exponents of 'logical monism.'
political_social_context: Spinoza's Tractatus Theologico-Politicus and Tractatus Politicus develop a Hobbesian view that the sovereign can do no wrong and the Church should be subordinate to the State, but Spinoza departs from Hobbes in favoring democracy as the 'most natural' government and in insisting subjects retain some rights, including freedom of opinion - made possible in practice by the relative toleration of the Dutch Republic.
religion_science_culture_context: Spinoza was excommunicated by the Amsterdam Jewish community and reviled by Christians as an atheist despite - or because of - a philosophy entirely centered on the idea of God; his biblical criticism anticipated modern scholarship by dating Old Testament books later than tradition held.
russell_presentation: Russell calls Spinoza 'the noblest and most lovable of the great philosophers' and, ethically, supreme among them, even though intellectually others surpassed him. He recounts Spinoza's simple, principled life - refusing a bribe to hide his views, surviving an assassination attempt, living modestly as a lens-grinder - as living proof that Spinoza practiced what he preached, dying as calmly as he had lived. Russell walks through the Ethics' three parts (metaphysics, psychology of the passions, and ethics), presenting the metaphysics as a modification of Descartes reduced to a single substance, the psychology as Hobbesian and egoistic, and the ethics - centered on understanding, freedom from fear, and the intellectual love of God - as the most valuable part of the book. Russell is explicit that the geometrical method of proof, however tedious, was essential to Spinoza's system rather than an affectation. He ultimately judges that the metaphysics must be rejected as incompatible with modern logic and scientific method, but that Spinoza's ethical maxims about facing death, misfortune, and the limits of human power calmly - while narrower than Spinoza himself claimed given his denial of free will - remain among the best available, even though Russell personally cannot accept Spinoza's claim that hatred can always be overcome by love, or that particular evils are dissolved by being 'part of the whole.'
key_takeaways: Spinoza reduces Descartes's three substances (God, mind, matter) to a single infinite substance, 'God or Nature,' of which minds and bodies are merely aspects.
His system is rigidly deterministic: there is no free will or chance, and everything follows with logical necessity from God's nature.
He answers the problem of evil by claiming that only the negative, limited aspect of an act (visible from a finite viewpoint) is 'evil'; God, being wholly positive, knows no evil.
Freedom consists in understanding: an emotion stops being an enslaving 'passion' once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
The highest human good is the 'intellectual love of God' - joy fused with the understanding that everything is part of the single necessary whole.
Russell rejects Spinoza's metaphysics as incompatible with modern logic and empirical science, but finds much of value in his ethical counsel about facing death and misfortune.
study_notes:
The key to reading this chapter is to keep Spinoza's three-part structure firmly in mind: metaphysics grounds psychology, and psychology grounds ethics. Everything Spinoza says about how to live follows, by his own geometrical method, from his claim that only one substance truly exists. If you accept that individual selves are not really separate things but 'modes' of one infinite being, then it starts to make sense why Spinoza thinks personal identity, personal grievance, and even personal death should matter to us far less than we naturally think they do - our apparent separateness is, on this view, something like an optical illusion produced by looking at only part of reality.

It is worth separating two very different kinds of claims Spinoza makes, because Russell insists on this separation too. One kind is strictly metaphysical: that there is one substance, that everything is logically necessary, that time is unreal from God's perspective. Russell thinks essentially none of this survives contact with modern science, which infers the world from observation rather than deducing it from self-evident axioms. The other kind of claim is practical and ethical: face death calmly, do not let hope and fear about an uncertain future dominate you, try to understand your emotions rather than being swept along by them. Russell thinks a surprising amount of this advice remains useful and admirable even once you have thrown out the metaphysical scaffolding that was supposed to prove it.

Finally, notice how Russell uses Spinoza to test a serious moral question: is it right to respond to atrocity with philosophical calm? Russell raises deliberately extreme wartime examples (a massacred family, a murdered spouse) to push on Spinoza's claim that seeing misfortune 'as part of the whole' should dissolve our grief and anger. His answer is genuinely mixed - he thinks Spinoza's redirection of attention toward larger matters can be a real comfort in extremity, but he refuses to agree that a cruel act somehow becomes less bad, or ceases to be a permanent black mark on the universe, just because it is absorbed into a larger cosmic pattern.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Something that exists in its own right and does not depend on anything else to exist.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Spinoza, that which is 'in itself and conceived through itself'; Spinoza argues there can be only one such substance, God or Nature.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A particular way in which the one substance shows up - like a wave is a particular shape water takes.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A finite, dependent modification or aspect of the single infinite substance; individual minds and bodies are modes, not substances, for Spinoza.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that God and the universe (Nature) are the same thing, rather than God being separate from and above the world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, exemplified by Spinoza's 'Deus sive Natura,' that identifies God with the single, all-encompassing substance of reality.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The natural drive every living thing has to keep existing and protect itself.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Spinoza's principle that everything, insofar as it is in itself, endeavors to persevere in its own being; the root of the passions in Book III of the Ethics.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An emotion you experience passively, as something happening to you from outside, rather than something you understand and control.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An emotion arising from inadequate (confused) ideas; it ceases to be a passion once the mind forms a clear and distinct idea of it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Latin for 'under the aspect of eternity' - looking at events as timeless facts rather than as things happening 'now' versus 'then.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Spinoza's ideal standpoint of reason, which views all events as part of the eternal, necessary order rather than privileging present or future over past.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, how does Spinoza's single-substance metaphysics differ from Descartes's view of substance?
questions.answer: Descartes allowed three substances (God, mind, and matter), with mind and matter treated as independent of each other; Spinoza collapses these into a single substance, 'God or Nature,' of which thought and extension are merely two of infinitely many attributes, and individual minds and bodies are not independent things but adjectival modes of that one substance.
questions.explanation: This is the foundational metaphysical move of the chapter, from which Spinoza's determinism and ethics both follow.

questions.prompt: How does Spinoza attempt to reconcile the existence of apparent evil (such as Nero's matricide) with a universe wholly determined by a perfect God?
questions.answer: He argues that what is positive in any act is good, and only its negative, limited aspect - visible only from a finite creature's partial viewpoint - appears evil; God, being wholly positive and real, has no knowledge of evil at all.
questions.explanation: Russell presents this as logically consistent with Spinoza's system but notes it cannot be reconciled with orthodox doctrines of sin and damnation.

questions.prompt: Compare Spinoza's view of emotion and freedom with the Stoic view, as Russell presents them.
questions.answer: The Stoics rejected virtually all emotion as something to be suppressed; Spinoza does not object to emotion as such, only to 'passions' - emotions that arise from inadequate, confused ideas and make us passive. An emotion ceases to be a passion, and we become correspondingly freer, once we understand it clearly and distinctly.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly distinguishes Spinoza from the Stoics on this point.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher did Russell say 'owed much to' Spinoza but concealed the debt and lied about the extent of his acquaintance with him?
questions.explanation: Leibniz visited Spinoza in 1676 and obtained part of the Ethics in manuscript, but later minimized the relationship out of caution.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct, in your own words, Spinoza's geometrical argument (as Russell presents it) for why love of God must hold the chief place in the mind.
questions.answer: The mind can refer all its bodily images and modifications to the idea of God; anyone who clearly understands himself and his emotions thereby loves God, and does so more as his understanding grows; and an idea occupies the mind more fully the more objects it is connected to. Since increasing understanding consists precisely in referring more and more things to God, love of God (understanding) must come to occupy the chief place in the mind.
questions.explanation: Russell quotes the actual geometrical proof and then restates it in plain language to show it is a logical deduction rather than a moral exhortation.

questions.prompt: What ultimate judgment does Russell reach about Spinoza's philosophy as a whole?
questions.answer: Russell rejects Spinoza's metaphysics as incompatible with modern logic and scientific method (since facts must be discovered by observation, not derived from self-evident axioms), but holds that much of his ethics - especially his counsel on facing death and personal misfortune calmly - can still be valuable even once the metaphysical foundation is rejected.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's explicit concluding evaluation near the end of the chapter.

flashcards.front: What does 'Deus sive Natura' mean, and whose doctrine is it?
flashcards.back: 'God or Nature' - Spinoza's phrase identifying God with the single infinite substance that makes up all of reality.

flashcards.front: How many substances did Descartes recognize, and how many did Spinoza recognize?
flashcards.back: Descartes: three (God, mind, matter). Spinoza: one (God/Nature), of which mind and matter are merely two known attributes.

flashcards.front: What is Spinoza's principle 'all determination is negation' used to prove?
flashcards.back: That finite things, being defined by their limits, cannot be wholly real; only one absolutely infinite, wholly positive being can exist - leading to pantheistic monism.

flashcards.front: Did Spinoza believe in free will?
flashcards.back: No - his system is rigidly deterministic; everything, mental and physical, follows from God's nature with the same necessity as a mathematical truth.

flashcards.front: How does Spinoza answer the objection that his determinism makes evil acts 'good' since God decrees everything?
flashcards.back: He distinguishes the positive aspect of an act (real, and therefore good) from its negative aspect (evil, but only from a finite, partial viewpoint); God, being wholly positive, knows no evil.

flashcards.front: What is a 'passion' in Spinoza's technical sense, and how do we escape it?
flashcards.back: An emotion arising from inadequate, confused ideas, in which we are passively driven by outside causes; it ceases to be a passion once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.

flashcards.front: What is the 'intellectual love of God' for Spinoza?
flashcards.back: A union of true understanding and joy that arises as the mind refers more and more of reality to the idea of God; Spinoza calls it the mind's highest good and virtue.

flashcards.front: What does sub specie aeternitatis mean, and why does it matter to Spinoza's ethics?
flashcards.back: 'Under the aspect of eternity' - viewing events timelessly rather than as more or less important depending on when they occur; it grounds Spinoza's view that hope and fear about the future are irrational.

flashcards.front: How did Spinoza make his living, and how did he respond to the offer of 1000 florins to hide his doubts?
flashcards.back: He made his living polishing lenses and refused the bribe, after which an unsuccessful attempt was made to assassinate him.

flashcards.front: According to Russell, what does Spinoza's political theory borrow from Hobbes, and where does it differ?
flashcards.back: It borrows the idea that the sovereign can do no wrong and the Church should be subordinate to the State, but differs in favoring democracy as the 'most natural' government and in insisting subjects should retain rights such as freedom of opinion.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's overall verdict on Spinoza's metaphysics versus his ethics?
flashcards.back: Russell rejects the metaphysics as incompatible with modern logic and scientific method, but thinks parts of the ethics - especially on facing death and misfortune - remain valuable even without the metaphysical foundation.

flashcards.front: Why, according to Russell, does he personally disagree with Spinoza's claim that particular evils dissolve when seen as 'part of the whole'?
flashcards.back: Russell argues that particular events are what they are and do not become different by absorption into a whole - a cruel act remains eternally a part of the universe regardless of later events.

quiz.prompt: How does Russell describe Spinoza ethically, compared with other great philosophers?
options: As the most logically rigorous but ethically unremarkable
As the noblest and most lovable, ethically supreme even if others surpassed him intellectually
As primarily important for his contributions to mathematics
As a minor figure overshadowed by Descartes
quiz.explanation: Russell opens the chapter calling Spinoza 'the noblest and most lovable of the great philosophers,' supreme ethically even though others surpassed him intellectually.

quiz.prompt: How many fundamental substances does Spinoza's metaphysics recognize?
options: Three, as in Descartes
Two: mind and matter
One: God or Nature
An infinite number of independent souls
quiz.explanation: Spinoza reduces Descartes's three substances to a single substance, God or Nature, of which mind and matter are merely attributes.

quiz.prompt: What style of exposition does Spinoza use in the Ethics, and why does Russell say this was not merely a stylistic quirk?
options: Dialogue form, because he wanted to dramatize disagreement
The geometrical method of Euclid, because it was essential to his claim that everything could be rigorously demonstrated
Personal letters, because he distrusted formal philosophy
Aphorisms, in imitation of Heraclitus
quiz.explanation: Russell explains that the geometrical method (definitions, axioms, theorems) was bound up with the essence of Spinoza's system, which held that everything could be demonstrated.

quiz.prompt: According to Spinoza's psychology of the passions in Book III of the Ethics, what is the fundamental motive underlying love, hate, and strife?
options: A desire to please God
The endeavor of everything to persevere in its own being (conatus)
Fear of death alone
Pure altruism
quiz.explanation: Spinoza's psychology of the passions is presented as fundamentally egoistic, rooted in the principle that everything endeavors to persevere in its own being.

quiz.prompt: Spinoza, like the Stoics, holds that all emotion should be suppressed.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly notes Spinoza does not object to all emotions as the Stoics did, only to 'passions' - emotions rooted in inadequate ideas.

quiz.prompt: In Spinoza's geometrical proof that 'love towards God must hold the chief place in the mind,' what role does proposition V, 11 play?
options: It defines God as the most perfect being
It states that a mental image occupies the mind more, the more objects it is referred to
It proves the existence of the external world
It establishes the identity of indiscernibles
quiz.explanation: Russell quotes Ethics V, 11, which states that a mental image is more frequent and vivid, and occupies the mind more, in proportion as it is referred to more objects - a key step in the proof.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's own criticism of Spinoza's claim that particular misfortunes are dissolved when seen as part of the whole?
options: He thinks it is logically inconsistent with the geometrical method
He argues that particular events are what they are and do not become different by absorption into a whole - a cruel act remains eternally part of the universe
He argues Spinoza's God does not really exist
He claims Spinoza never actually applied this idea to real suffering
quiz.explanation: Russell states directly that he cannot accept this doctrine because particular events do not change their character by being absorbed into a larger whole.

quiz.prompt: Spinoza made his living by ________ while devoting his intellectual life to philosophy.
options: teaching at a university
polishing lenses
practicing medicine
working as a merchant
quiz.explanation: Russell notes Spinoza lived quietly making his living by polishing lenses, showing his indifference to money.

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell rejects Spinoza's metaphysics but praises much of his ethics. Using the chapter's evidence, evaluate whether Spinoza's ethical counsel (on death, misfortune, and the passions) can really be detached from the metaphysical claim that everything is logically necessary, or whether the ethics ultimately depends on the metaphysics being true.
rubric: Accurately summarizes Spinoza's metaphysics and ethics as Russell presents them
Engages with Russell's own attempted separation of the two
Considers whether determinism is doing real work in the ethical arguments

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Spinoza's solution to the problem of evil (the 'negation' argument) with the objections Russell raises against it, including his own wartime examples of atrocity. Which do you find more persuasive, and why?
rubric: Uses specific textual evidence from the chapter
